results.title: Machine Safety Fundamentals: Emergency Stop
results.content: # Machine Safety Fundamentals: Emergency Stop. An emergency stop, also known as an e-stop, is a safety feature implemented in industrial machinery and automation systems. The main function of the e-stop is to halt all potentially dangerous movements or processes as swiftly and safely as possible during an emergency situation. Upon activation, most e-stops initiate a Category 1 stop, where the actuator or motor is brought to a controlled halt. E-stops are an essential safety component in industrial automation and machinery, providing protection for both workers and equipment in emergency situations. Before operating a new e-stop application, be sure to consult the standards or a safety expert who understands the standards and the specific application. E-stops are meant to operate as quickly as possible in an emergency situation, so visibility is key. The actuation of an emergency-stop device must be from a single manual action, such as pressing a push button or pulling a cable. The emergency stop of hazardous motion should not create new hazards, such as upsetting a load. An emergency stop device should be located at each operator control station, and a risk assessment should determine other appropriate locations for the particular application. E-stops are commonly found at entrance and exit locations or where operators and machines work together. Operators should have immediate access to emergency-stop devices for quick activation. The scope of an e-stop’s control is determined by the machines and their application. These controls include interlock devices, presence-sensing devices, enabling devices, hold-to-run controls, resets, and emergency stops. An emergency-stop actuator should be a maintained device. Once triggered, the e-stop stays in effect until it is manually reset, ensuring that the machinery remains halted until it is deliberately reset. Functional testing should periodically trigger the e-stop function, following the manufacturer’s guidelines, and confirm that the machinery halts. Any maintained mechanisms should be tested and the e-stop control reset confirmed. The testing frequency needs to strike a balance between the stresses that e-stop activation imposes on the equipment—whether mechanical, electrical, or fluid power—and ensuring that the e-stop operates correctly. 4. results.title: What is an emergency stop? | Control Design
results.content: # What is an emergency stop? An emergency stop (e-stop) is a safety mechanism used in industrial machines and automation systems. When activated, most e-stops initiate a Cat. 1 stop in which the actuator/motor is brought to a controlled stop. “An emergency stop should be initiated by a single manual action,” says Mark Eitzman, safety and product manager at Integrated Mills Systems in Willoughby, Ohio. Many standards guide the use and operations of e-stops, such as International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 13850 “Safety of machinery—Emergency stop function—Principles for design,” as well as NFPA 79, “Electrical Standard for Industrial Machinery,” and IEC 60204-1, Safety of machinery – Electrical equipment of machines. E-stops are meant to operate as quickly as possible in an emergency situation, so visibility is key. The actuation of an emergency-stop device must be from a single manual action, such as pressing a push button or pulling a cable. • Category 0 is an uncontrolled stop which immediately removes power to the machine actuators. • Category 1 is a controlled stop with power to the machine actuators available to achieve the stop. ### Where should emergency-stop devices be located? An emergency stop device should be located at each operator control station, and a risk assessment should determine other appropriate locations for the particular application. E-stops are commonly found at entrance and exit locations or where operators and machine work together. Emergency-stop devices should be directly accessible to operators for easy actuation. The machines and application will determine an e-stop’s span of control. “An emergency-stop actuator shall be a maintained mechanism,” Eitzman says. Other control functions or systems should never override an emergency-stop command. “The twisting and/or pulling out the depressed actuator is a common feature used to reset the e-stop button,” says Eitzman. Test any maintained mechanisms and confirm the e-stop control resets. Emergency-stop equipment—safety-related parts of a control system which perform the emergency-stop function (Source: ISO 13850, 3.2). Emergency-stop device—manually actuated control device used to initiate an emergency-stop function (Source: IEC 60947‑5‑5:2005, 3.2). Span of control of emergency-stop device—predetermined section of the machinery under control of specific emergency-stop devices (Source: ISO 13850, 3.6].

results.title: Issue Brief: Thresholds for Frontier AI Safety Frameworks - Frontier Model Forum
results.content: Within AI safety frameworks, thresholds describe predefined notions of risk that indicate when additional action is warranted to avoid unacceptable outcomes.2 Although they may be operationalized in different ways, thresholds provide a structured approach to managing risk by establishing clear boundaries for acceptable levels of risk and a process to keep risks within tolerable levels.3 Setting thresholds in advance of development enables all actors across the frontier AI development lifecycle, including developers, deployers, and regulators, to play their part in addressing any potential hazards before they materialize. By establishing concrete standards for acceptable levels of risk and identifying key outcomes of concern, thresholds enable more efficient internal decision-making processes by frontier AI developers and providers, as well as any potential external oversight that may be required. Without predefined thresholds, decisions about AI safety measures may become more ad hoc, making it difficult to weigh tradeoffs around the benefits and risks associated with frontier AI models and systems. There are several main approaches to establishing thresholds within frontier AI safety frameworks, each of which entails a unique set of tradeoffs. * ***Risk thresholds*** set explicit limits for acceptable levels of the estimated risk stemming from the deployment of a frontier AI model or system. For instance, ***outcome-based thresholds*** specify a set of outcomes that represent the intolerable threshold, along with a set of threat scenarios that describe how a frontier AI model could be misused to produce those outcomes.8 Assessments are designed to test whether a frontier AI model could uniquely enable a threat scenario, and to measure the level of risk a model poses towards realizing these intolerable outcomes. Moreover, capability thresholds are more straightforward to measure than risk thresholds, which are currently difficult to estimate for frontier AI. Capability thresholds therefore offer an effective compromise between risk and compute thresholds, and can inform determinations about the safety of a given AI system even when risk estimates remain uncertain. Thresholds are a critical component of frontier AI safety frameworks, providing clear guidelines for when additional safety measures must be implemented during AI development. Further research is needed to address these questions and enable frontier AI developers and providers to implement safety framework thresholds more effectively.

results.title: Beyond Alignment: What Safety-Critical Industries Can Teach Us About Safe AI Development | by Elif Ayvali | Medium
results.content: While discussions of AI safety often focus on alignment challenges and theoretical risks, many real-world AI incidents originate from something far more mundane: poor change management, inadequate validation, and missing quality controls. These industries have comprehensive safety and quality management frameworks which provide systematic approaches to handling uncertainty and potential failures from initial design through deployment and maintenance. * How do we evaluate if safety controls are sufficient as systems scale? ***Risk Identification:*** Safety-critical industries use well-established methods to identify and address risks. Among these, System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) in particular is relevant for analyzing AI systems, as it examines control system safety and complex interactions between components (e.g., base model, RLHF mechanisms, safety filters, user interfaces, monitoring systems). * **Technical risk factors**: Complexity in model architecture, training pipeline design, deployment configurations, operational volume, user access patterns, and integration with other critical systems. Leading AI organizations implement diverse risk assessment frameworks to manage potential harms from advanced systems. These frameworks emphasize only the most extreme, long-term hazards, lacking systematic hazard analysis, criteria to detect exposure or severity in operational deployments, and clear thresholds for when safety policies themselves require updating. * **Regular Updates:** Conduct periodic safety case reviews, schedule routine internal evaluations and independent audits, and maintain up-to-date risk assessments based on operational data. * **Review Gates:** Set clear criteria for when additional safety reviews are required (e.g., new risk categories, significant architectural changes, deployment to new domains). Safety-critical industries rely on formal Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) process that includes:. Organizations need a formal framework to implement and verify safety requirements. Design controls create clear linkages between safety requirements, their implementation, and evidence that they work as intended. In reality, the safety practices can and should scale with your system’s complexity and risk profile. Automated testing pipelines, formal incident tracking systems, and periodic safety reviews ensure that practices evolve alongside product complexity. For global deployments handling healthcare or critical infrastructure, systems need continuous monitoring and potentially geographic risk analysis. Whether you are building LLMs or deploying smaller-scale AI systems, which safety practice will you bring into your workflows today?

results.content: # How do you design an emergency stop circuit for an e-stop switch? ### How can you implement an emergency stop circuit for an e-stop switch (with circuit diagrams)? According to EN ISO 13850, each machine (with the exception of hand-held and hand-operated machines) must have an emergency stop function which can be initiated by a single human action. This e-stop function must be initiated by an appropriate controlled stop device: By actuating an emergency stop switch or an emergency stop switch, the existing hazard is switched off via safety switchgear. ### Requirements for an emergency stop circuit:. ## Practical examples for simple emergency stop circuits. ### **Emergency stop circuit in the main circuit**. ### **Emergency stop circuit in the control circuit**. The control circuit can also be used to implement an emergency stop circuit or an emergency shutdown for stopping machines and systems in the event of a hazard. The safety contactor/contactor Q1 is de-energised by pressing the emergency stop button S1. The internal logic of the safety relays monitors the safety circuits (emergency stop, protective door) and activates the enabling-current paths if no faults are detected. For extensive control systems in which several electrical circuits must be interrupted, and where hazards to the operator or machine can arise, you can use a safety relay to achieve an emergency shutdown. The required emergency stop circuit can be quickly implemented using pre-designed and verified safety function blocks. * Bridging in the emergency stop button or in the input wiring leads to the loss of the safety feature. ### **Dual-channel emergency stop with safety relay**.
